title: Functionally-Complete Boolean Logic in Real DRAM Chips: Experimental Characterization and Analysis
problem: Prior work on Processing-using-DRAM (PuD) has only demonstrated limited Boolean operations (3-input MAJ, 2-input AND/OR) in commercial DRAM chips without providing a functionally complete set. The challenge is to experimentally demonstrate functionally-complete Boolean operations (NOT, NAND, NOR) and many-input operations (more than two inputs) in off-the-shelf DRAM chips with acceptable reliability.
motivation: In-DRAM computation through PuD architectures can significantly reduce costly data movement between processing elements and main memory by enabling massively parallel computation directly in DRAM.
method: The authors experimentally characterize bulk bitwise Boolean operations in 256 off-the-shelf DDR4 DRAM chips by leveraging the analog operational properties of DRAM circuitry. They evaluate operation reliability using a success rate metric (fraction of correctly performed operations) and systematically test NOT, NAND, NOR, AND, and OR operations across varying input counts (up to 16 inputs), data patterns, and temperature ranges (50-95°C) to assess resilience and practical utility.
key_novelty: Demonstrating functionally-complete Boolean operations (NOT, NAND, NOR) with high reliability (>94%) and support for many-input variants (up to 16 inputs) in commercial off-the-shelf DRAM chips, enabling arbitrary Boolean computation directly in memory.
contributions: Experimental demonstration of NOT operation in COTS DRAM with 98.37% average success rate
Characterization of up to 16-input NAND, NOR, AND, OR operations with 94.94-95.87% average success rates
Analysis showing data patterns have minimal impact on operation reliability (1-2% variation)
Evaluation of high temperature resilience with at most 1.66% success rate fluctuation across 50-95°C range

metrics.accuracy: NOT: 98.37% success rate; 16-input NAND: 94.94%; 16-input NOR: 95.87%; 16-input AND: 94.94%; 16-input OR: 95.85%

limitations: Paper does not discuss power consumption, latency, or performance overhead of in-DRAM Boolean operations compared to traditional computation.
